name: Zinc-Cryonis
geological_features: Zinc-rich ice formations creating blue-white metallic surfaces
Frozen geysers forming towering ice spires
specific_features: Derelict space station in low orbit
description: Zinc-Cryonis is an ice world distinguished by the high zinc content of its ice formations, which gives the surface a distinctive blue-white metallic appearance quite unlike the pure white of standard water ice. The frozen geysers have built towering spires of zinc-rich ice that reach hundreds of meters into the thin atmosphere, their surfaces catching the light with a cold metallic gleam. A subterranean ocean beneath the ice sheet supports hydrothermal ecosystems that include the only known extraterrestrial cold-adapted flora.

The metallic quality of the ice creates an environment that feels more like walking through a frozen industrial landscape than a natural world. The ice spires ring when struck, producing clear bell-like tones that carry for kilometers in the still, cold air, and some explorers have composed crude melodies by striking different spires in sequence. The thin atmosphere supports spectacular stellar views, and the zinc-ice surface reflects starlight with enough intensity to navigate by even on moonless nights.

A terraforming initiative was begun here with the intent of thickening the atmosphere and warming the surface enough to create a habitable world. The project was halted when the unique subterranean flora was discovered, as the warming process would destroy the delicate ecosystem before it could be fully studied. The terraforming equipment remains in standby mode, maintained by automated systems, a half-completed promise of transformation that the flora's defenders have fought to keep unfulfilled.

The subterranean flora produces compounds found nowhere else, including antifreeze proteins with medical applications that have proven effective against several previously untreatable neurological conditions. The endangered status of these organisms makes them both scientifically priceless and commercially valuable, creating a tension between conservation and exploitation. The terraforming debate has become a proxy for larger philosophical questions about whether uninhabited worlds have intrinsic value or exist primarily as resources for modification.
